title: Reactor Pattern
oneLiner: Handles many concurrent I/O sources with a single thread, dispatching to the right handler the instant each one is ready.

hero.name: The Watchtower
hero.catchphrase: One thread, watching everything, dispatching the instant it's ready.
hero.power: Watches many I/O sources at once from a single thread, dispatching each event to its registered handler the moment it's ready.
hero.weakness: One slow or blocking handler stalls the entire event loop — every other connection waits behind it.
hero.origin: The Watchtower appeared after a server spawned a new thread per connection and collapsed under 10,000 simultaneous clients, each thread eating memory just to sit idle waiting for data.

story.problem: A server spawns one thread per client connection. At 10,000 concurrent connections, most idle and waiting, the server runs out of memory just from thread overhead.
story.solution: The Watchtower replaces one-thread-per-connection with a single event loop that watches all sockets at once, using the OS's readiness notification (like `epoll`) to know exactly when each socket has data.
story.result: One thread now handles all 10,000 connections. CPU and memory usage scale with actual activity, not the raw connection count.

before: One OS thread allocated per connection, mostly idle
Memory and context-switch overhead scale with connection count
Thousands of idle threads for thousands of idle connections
after: One thread watches every connection via readiness notification
Memory scales with actual activity, not connection count
Thousands of idle connections cost almost nothing

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A server monitor shows 10,000 threads, 9,900 of them idle, all eating memory just waiting for data.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We're out of memory and 99% of these threads are just sitting there, doing absolutely nothing but waiting.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Watchtower appears on one high perch, scanning every connection at once.
panels.speaker: The Watchtower
panels.dialogue: You don't need a thread per connection. Give me one thread — I'll watch everything, and only wake up work when there's actually something ready.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: One event loop asks the OS which sockets have data ready, then dispatches to each socket's registered handler.
panels.speaker: The Watchtower
panels.dialogue: The OS tells me exactly who's ready. I dispatch to the right handler instantly, then go back to watching everyone else.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The same server now handles 10,000 idle connections on one thread with minimal memory.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One thread, 10,000 connections, and memory usage barely moved. The idle ones cost us almost nothing now.

useWhen: You need to handle a very large number of mostly-idle concurrent connections (chat servers, long-poll APIs, IoT device fleets).
Thread-per-connection overhead (memory, context switching) is the actual bottleneck.
I/O readiness notification is available from the OS or runtime (epoll, kqueue, IOCP, or a language runtime built on them).
avoidWhen: Connection counts are small enough that thread-per-connection isn't actually a problem.
Handlers do genuinely CPU-heavy work — a Reactor's single thread means one slow handler blocks everyone else.
The platform/runtime doesn't provide efficient readiness notification, making a hand-rolled reactor slower than the alternative.
commonMistakes: Putting CPU-bound or blocking work directly in a Reactor handler, stalling the entire event loop for every other connection.
Reimplementing a Reactor from scratch instead of using a mature runtime that already provides one (Node.js, Netty, nginx all have battle-tested reactors built in).
Not handling partial reads/writes correctly, since non-blocking I/O may return less data than expected on any given call.
Confusing Reactor (notified when I/O is ready to be performed) with Proactor (notified when I/O is already complete).
explanation.realWorldExample: Node.js's event loop, nginx's connection handling, Redis's single-threaded event loop, and Java NIO's Selector are all real-world Reactor implementations.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: This sounds like it's just... Node.js's whole architecture.

conversation.speaker: The Watchtower
conversation.message: Exactly right — Node's entire event loop is a Reactor. One thread, watching everything, dispatching callbacks the instant something's ready to read or write.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What's my biggest risk running on top of you?

conversation.speaker: The Watchtower
conversation.message: Blocking me. If your handler does something slow — CPU-heavy computation, a synchronous file read — every other connection on my one thread waits behind it. Keep handlers fast, or offload heavy work elsewhere.

codeBattle.scenario: Your chat server needs to handle 50,000 simultaneous idle WebSocket connections, most sending a message only once every few minutes, on a machine with limited memory.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Watchtower handles all 50,000 mostly-idle connections on one thread via readiness notification, instead of allocating a thread per connection that would exhaust memory.

quiz.question: What is the core mechanism a Reactor relies on?
options: OS-level readiness notification telling it which I/O sources have data waiting
A separate thread for every connection
Polling every connection in a tight loop, constantly
quiz.answer: OS-level readiness notification telling it which I/O sources have data waiting
quiz.explanation: Mechanisms like epoll/kqueue/IOCP let the Reactor efficiently know exactly which sockets are ready, without busy-polling.

quiz.question: What's the single biggest risk of using a Reactor?
options: A slow or blocking handler stalls the entire event loop, delaying every other connection
It requires one thread per connection
It can only handle a single connection at a time
It cannot be combined with any other pattern
quiz.answer: A slow or blocking handler stalls the entire event loop, delaying every other connection
quiz.explanation: Because one thread services every registered event, any handler that blocks holds up all the others.

quiz.question: How does Reactor differ from Proactor?
options: Reactor notifies when I/O is ready to be performed; Proactor notifies when the I/O operation has already completed
They are identical patterns with different names
Proactor requires multiple threads; Reactor forbids threads entirely
Reactor can only be used for file I/O
quiz.answer: Reactor notifies when I/O is ready to be performed; Proactor notifies when the I/O operation has already completed
quiz.explanation: This readiness-vs-completion distinction is exactly what separates the two closely related concurrency patterns.

quiz.question: What's a well-known real-world Reactor implementation?
options: A relational database's transaction isolation level
quiz.explanation: Node.js's single-threaded, callback-dispatching event loop is one of the most widely used Reactor implementations in practice.
